rules.title: Berkeley prohibition on the sale or use of coordinated pricing algorithms to set rents or manage occupancy (BMC ch. 13.63)
rules.requirement:
It is unlawful to sell, license or otherwise provide to Berkeley landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley. It is also unlawful for a landlord to use such an algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels.

A coordinated pricing algorithm is any analytical or computational process that uses Competitor Data to calculate and recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other rental contract terms for future leases. The coordination is between a Berkeley landlord and one or more competitors, including through a third-party vendor. Competitor Data is nonpublic rent, occupancy, lease-date and similar data on properties the landlord does not own or manage, when the data is less than 90 days old.

Each month a violation continues, and each unit for which the algorithm was used, is a separate violation.

Enforcement:
- The City Attorney may sue for damages, injunctive relief, restitution of illegal profits and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
- An aggrieved tenant may sue a landlord user for injunctive relief, money damages and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
- A prevailing City Attorney or tenant receives mandatory attorney's fees and costs. Lease clauses limiting a tenant's fees are unenforceable.

The chapter does not regulate the amount of rent a landlord may charge.

rules.requirement:
An owner or agent who charges an applicant a fee for a consumer credit report and application processing must disclose two things, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee (BMC 13.78.010):
- a clear and conspicuous Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement;
- the maximum fee cap under Civ. Code § 1950.6(b).

An owner may not charge an existing tenant a non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy, including fees tied to a roommate's departure or a request to add or replace a roommate (BMC 13.78.016).

The chapter applies to all residential rental agreements regardless of contrary lease terms, and conflicting lease provisions are unenforceable (BMC 13.78.018).

The dollar cap, receipt, credit-report copy and refund rules are state law (Civ. Code § 1950.6).

rules.title: California application screening fee cap, receipt and refund rules (Civ. Code § 1950.6)
rules.requirement:
A landlord or agent may charge an applicant, including a guarantor or cosigner, an application screening fee only to cover actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information, plus the reasonable value of time. The fee may not exceed $30 per applicant, adjustable annually by CPI from January 1, 1998.

No fee may be charged when the landlord knows or should know that no unit is available or will be available within a reasonable time.

A fee may be charged only if the landlord offers one of two processes:
(A) First-qualified-applicant processing. Applications are considered in the order received under written criteria, and no fee is charged until an application is actually considered. Fees collected inadvertently from concurrent submissions are refunded within 7 days.
(B) Full refund to every applicant not selected, within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first.

After collecting a fee, the landlord must:
- give an itemized receipt
- return any unused fee if no reference check or credit report is obtained
- give the applicant a copy of the credit report within 7 days of receiving it

A reusable screening report may be accepted. The fee is not 'security' under § 1950.5. Rules for federal or state housing-assistance programs are not preempted.

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (DND-funded and inclusionary housing)
rules.requirement:
The policy applies to housing providers that receive DND funding or land, or that have income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy. These providers may not impose a blanket denial based on arrests or convictions and must assess applicants case by case.

When deciding eligibility or considering eviction, providers may not consider:
- arrests that did not result in a conviction;
- convictions subject to judicial relief, such as expungement, sealing or certificates of relief;
- juvenile records;
- convictions more than 5 years old.

These limits do not apply where there is a direct relationship between the conviction and the housing sought, an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety, or current criminal behavior.

Credit rules:
- Providers may not use credit scores to approve or deny applications.
- Credit history may be used only in place of rental history when rental history is unavailable.
- Lack of credit history alone is not grounds for rejection.

Providers should weigh mitigating factors and, where feasible, offer an appeals process. Conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements preempt the policy.

rules.title: Cartwright Act prohibition on common pricing algorithms (AB 325, Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729)
rules.requirement:
It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce.

It is also unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm while coercing another person to adopt its recommended price or commercial term for the same or similar products or services in California.

Definitions:
- A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including software or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set or otherwise influence a price or commercial term.
- Commercial terms include level of service, availability and output.
- 'Distribute' includes licensing and subscriptions.

The rule is general antitrust law, not housing-specific; per Cleary Gottlieb, apartment rental companies have been targets of federal algorithmic pricing claims. A companion section (§ 16756.1) lets a Cartwright Act complaint plead only plausible facts, without excluding the possibility of independent action. The section does not limit other antitrust law.
rules.key_value: Ban on use or distribution of common pricing algorithms in a restraint of trade or with coercion; Cartwright Act violations are punishable as a crime; per secondary source, criminal fines up to the greater of $6M (corporations) or $1M (individuals) or twice the gain or loss, and civil fines up to $1M in AG/DA actions (SB 763)

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act just-cause eviction (Civ. Code § 1946.2)
rules.requirement:
Once a tenant has lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the owner may terminate the tenancy only for just cause, which must be stated in the written notice. If an adult tenant was added before 24 months, the rule applies when all tenants have 12 months or any tenant has 24 months.

At-fault causes: nonpayment, material lease breach, nuisance, waste, refusal to renew a similar lease, criminal activity, unauthorized assignment or subletting, refusal of lawful entry, unlawful use, an employee's failure to vacate, and failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice. A curable violation requires a notice to cure before a 3-day notice to quit.

No-fault causes:
- Owner or relative move-in. The occupant must move in within 90 days and stay 12 months. For leases from July 1, 2020, the tenant must agree or the lease must allow it.
- Withdrawal from the rental market.
- Government or court vacate order.
- Demolition or substantial remodel requiring at least 30 consecutive days of vacancy, with the specified notice contents.

For any no-fault termination, the owner must either pay relocation of one month's rent within 15 days or waive the final month's rent, and must state this right in the notice.

Owners must give tenants a prescribed notice of these rights. Noncompliance voids the notice. Tenants may recover actual damages, attorney's fees, and up to 3x damages for willful violations. The Attorney General and local prosecutors may seek injunctions. Waivers are void.
rules.key_value: Just cause after 12 months (24 months if an adult tenant was added); no-fault relocation = 1 month's rent within 15 calendar days or waiver of the final month's rent; owner move-in occupant within 90 days for 12 months; remodel requires at least 30 consecutive days vacated; up to 3x actual damages for willful violations; repealed Jan. 1, 2030

A security deposit may not exceed the first month's rent. Holding and paperwork:
- Hold it in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act: criminal-record screening limits
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not put criminal-record questions on an application, or ask about criminal records orally or in writing, before a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration. At no stage may a provider evaluate arrests or charges without conviction, expunged convictions, pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications or sealed records. After a conditional offer, a provider may consider only: (1) convictions for listed serious crimes or offenses requiring lifetime registration, and (2) indictable offenses within the lookback periods. A conditional offer may be withdrawn only if the provider finds, by a preponderance of the evidence, that withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate and nondiscriminatory interest. The provider must first make an individualized assessment. Withdrawal requires written notice giving specific reasons and an opportunity to appeal. The applicant may request, within 30 days, the information the provider relied on, and the provider must supply it free within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy, rehabilitation or mitigation. Discriminatory advertising about criminal records is barred, as is misuse or dissemination of records. Drug or alcohol tests, and consent to obtain drug-treatment information, may not be required. Landlords are immune from civil liability for renting to people with records or for not screening. Enforcement is only through complaints to the Division on Civil Rights, not in court. The Division first offers 14-day mediation. Penalties are capped at $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations. The director may also order return of the application fee and payment of up to $1,000 to the applicant.
rules.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; lookback 6 yrs (1st degree), 4 yrs (2nd/3rd degree), 1 yr (4th degree); no limit for murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, listed sex offenses or lifetime registration; records request within 30 days, provided free within 10 days; penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A landlord may collect a security deposit of no more than 1.5 times one month's rent. Any pet deposit and any prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, count toward this cap. At lease start, the landlord may require at most 2.5 months' rent: the deposit plus first month's rent. A yearly increase may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit remains the tenant's property and must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey institution, without commingling. Landlords holding deposits for 10 or more units may instead use certain insured money market funds. Interest belongs to the tenant. Within 30 days of receiving the deposit, and with each annual interest payment, the landlord must give written notice of the institution, amount, account type and rate. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may have the deposit plus 7% annual interest applied to rent. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit plus interest, less deductions itemized by registered or certified mail. Return is due within 5 business days if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation. A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus costs and attorney's fees.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not evict a tenant, or refuse to renew a lease, without good cause. The statutory causes are:
- nonpayment of rent
- disorderly conduct
- property damage
- substantial breach of rules or lease covenants
- failure to pay a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with local ordinances
- health and safety removal or government redevelopment
- permanent retirement from residential use
- refusal of reasonable lease changes
- habitual late payment
- condominium, cooperative or fee-simple conversion
- owner or buyer occupancy after conversion or in small buildings
- end of employment-based tenancy
- certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking offenses

A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment. Some causes also require a prior Notice to Cease, which has no statutory period but must allow reasonable time. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal can remove a tenant, and self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance of six times monthly rent. Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the same causes and notice rules. They must also give the County Welfare Board 3 working days' notice. Landlords who misuse a unit after an owner-occupancy or retirement eviction face treble damages. Residential reuse within 5 years after a retirement eviction can bring civil penalties up to $10,000.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (condominium/cooperative conversion protections)
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership, qualifying tenants may obtain protected tenancy, which protects them from eviction for up to 40 years. Qualifying tenants are those aged 62 or older before the conversion recording date, permanently disabled tenants, or service-disabled veterans rated 60% or higher. They must have lived in the building at least one year before the recording date. Family income must not exceed three times the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of the right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days. For all tenants in a converting building, whether protected or not, rents may not be raised to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Increases for new services or amenities remain allowed.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just-cause eviction and relocation payments (S.F. Admin. Code §§ 37.9(a), 37.9A, 37.9C)
rules.requirement:
A landlord of a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance may evict only for one of 17 just causes in § 37.9(a), and the just cause must be the dominant motive. Mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership is not just cause.

The causes are:
- nonpayment, habitual late payment or frequent bounced checks
- failure to cure a substantial breach
- severe or continuing nuisance
- illegal use
- refusal to sign a materially similar renewal
- refusal of lawful access
- unapproved subtenant remaining at the end of the term
- owner or relative move-in
- approved condominium conversion sale
- demolition or permanent removal from housing use
- temporary capital improvement work
- substantial rehabilitation of a building at least 50 years old, where cost is at least 75% of new construction
- Ellis Act withdrawal
- lead remediation
- demolition under a Chapter 56 development agreement
- expired Good Samaritan occupancy, with notice within 60 days
- demolition under Planning Code § 317

Just cause is also required to remove housing services such as parking, storage and laundry. Under § 37.2(r) a landlord may temporarily remove such services for mandatory soft-story seismic retrofit work.

Relocation under § 37.9C applies to evictions for owner or relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation. The landlord pays a per-tenant amount, capped per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant or household with minor children.

Relocation under § 37.9A applies to Ellis Act evictions. The landlord pays a per-tenant amount, capped per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant.

All relocation amounts adjust each March 1 and are fixed by the date the eviction notice is served. Temporary capital improvement displacement of less than 20 days is governed by Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9, not § 37.9C.

rules.title: San Francisco ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices (S.F. Admin. Code § 37.10C)
rules.requirement:
The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. An algorithmic device is, for example, a software program that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend the rent for a vacant unit.

A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action. Per a secondary source, tenants may seek damages, injunctive relief and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. Each month of use for each affected dwelling unit may be a separate violation.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance: annual rent increase cap
rules.requirement:
Annual residential rent increases are limited to the lower of 3% or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period. If the CPI is negative, no increase is permitted.

The City publishes the allowable increase by June 30 each year, effective September 1. The maximum allowable increase is 2.87% for September 1, 2026 through August 31, 2027.

Owners of residential rental property or a mobile home park may petition for relief from the cap by showing that a larger increase is needed for a fair and reasonable return. The City Manager or designee decides within 60 days of a complete application.

Tenants may petition to:
- contest increases above the maximum
- seek rent reductions for decreased housing services or habitability failures
- contest unauthorized or excessive capital-improvement pass-throughs
- report other violations

Landlords may, but need not, pass through the rental registration fee. The pass-through is capped at $50 per rental unit, not per tenant, and any overpayment must be reimbursed.

Owners must give written notice of the Ordinance and tenant rights at lease commencement or with any rent-increase notice.

rules.title: Preventing Algorithmic Rent-Fixing in the Rental Housing Market (§ 218-12, as amended by Ord. 25-076)
rules.requirement:
Real estate lessors, their agents and their subcontractors may not subscribe to, contract with, exchange anything of value for, or otherwise use the services of a Service Provider. The words "or otherwise utilize" were added by Ord. 25-076.

A Service Provider is any person that performs a coordination function for a real estate lessor. Coordination means three steps:
- collecting nonpublic competitor information from real estate lessors, together with historical or contemporaneous prices, price changes, supply levels, occupancy rates, or lease termination and renewal dates from two or more lessors or from public databases;
- analyzing or processing that information with a system, software or process that uses computation;
- recommending rental prices, lease terms or occupancy levels to a lessor.

Nonpublic competitor information is information less than 365 days old that is not widely and readily available to the public at no cost.

No service provider may facilitate an agreement not to compete among real estate lessors on any aspect of residential dwelling units, including rental pricing, fees or other rental terms.

Enforcement:
- The Attorney General or any municipal or county attorney may sue as parens patriae.
- The Office of Landlord-Tenant Affairs and the Office of Code Compliance enforce the section. Complaints go to the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations, which may refer them for prosecution.
- Any injured person has a private right of action.

A first violation is punishable under Jersey City Code § 1-25. Subsequent violations carry fines of $100 to $2,000, and each day of violation is a separate violation. Successful plaintiffs, including public enforcers, recover costs and reasonable attorney fees.

rules.requirement:

Measure BB limits on causes:
- Nonpayment eviction is allowed only if rental debt is at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent (Oakland-Fremont metro) for an equivalent unit.
- A tenant may not be evicted for refusing to sign a substantially similar new lease when a fixed-term lease expires.

Notice duties:
- Any termination notice must state that advice is available from the Rent Board and give its housing counseling phone number and website.
- Copies of termination notices, notices to quit and summons and complaints must be filed with the Rent Board within 3 business days of service.

Owner move-in evictions require relocation assistance, which the Rent Board must adjust for inflation each year. From Jan 1, 2026 the amounts are $19,413 standard plus $6,471 for qualifying households.

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Ordinance Annual General Adjustment cap (Measure BB 5% maximum; 2026 AGA 1.0%)
rules.requirement:
Landlords of fully covered units may raise the permanent rent ceiling each year only by the Annual General Adjustment (AGA) set by the Rent Board.

Formula and cap:
- The AGA is 65% of the Bay Area CPI-U increase (formula approved by voters in November 2004).
- Measure BB caps the AGA at 5%.
- Landlords with banked (unused) prior AGAs may still exceed 5% to reach the rent ceiling.

The 2026 AGA Order (Rent Board Regulation 1148), adopted October 16, 2025:
- Lets eligible landlords raise 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0%, no earlier than January 1, 2026.
- 1.0% is 65% of the 1.5% CPI increase for July 2024 to June 2025.
- Does not adjust rents for tenancies that began on or after January 1, 2025 with rents set under Costa-Hawkins.
- Regulation 1148 sets the qualifying conditions and the required notice to tenants.

Other Measure BB changes:
- Rent increases may be petitioned only for completed capital improvements.

rules.requirement:
Housing providers, including tenant screening companies, may check an applicant's criminal history, but with limits:
- They may not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile justice records.
- Blanket bans on applicants with any criminal history are prohibited.
- A denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and to not threaten the health and safety of others or property.
- In deciding whether a conviction is directly related, providers should weigh the nature and severity of the crime and the time elapsed since the conduct.

rules.title: Prohibition Against Algorithmic Rent-Fixing in the Rental Housing Market
rules.requirement: Landlords renting any residential dwelling unit in Hoboken may not price-fix using algorithmic pricing. This means using software, algorithms or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors in order to coordinate, recommend or implement rental prices, lease terms or occupancy levels among competing lessors. Nonpublic competitor information includes prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease termination and renewal dates, and other material terms that are less than 365 days old and not widely and readily available to the public at no cost. The Division of Housing, or any private citizen claiming to be aggrieved, may bring alleged violations to the Hoboken Municipal Court. On conviction, a violator faces one or more of the following: penalties under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5, a fine of up to $2,000, or community service of up to 90 days.

rules.title: Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO): annual allowable rent increase
rules.requirement:
In RSO units, rent may be raised once every 12 months by the allowable percentage published by LAHD. That percentage was 3% for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026.

Add-ons:
- From February 2, 2026, no extra percentage for utilities and no 10% add-on for an added dependent.
- A 10% increase for an additional non-dependent tenant is still allowed if taken within 60 days of the landlord learning of that tenant.

Increases above the allowable percentage need LAHD approval. The approval programs are capital improvement, primary renovation, seismic retrofit, rehabilitation, and just and reasonable rent increase.

Rent may go to market rate after any of these:
- a voluntary move-out
- eviction for nonpayment, lease violation, Tenant Habitability Plan noncompliance or a City Attorney order
- a Tenant Buyout Agreement

Rent increases were prohibited from March 30, 2020 through January 31, 2024.

Landlords may pass through these surcharges, separate from rent, only after registering the units and giving written notice:
- RSO registration surcharge: $1.61 per month
- SCEP surcharge: $2.83 per month
- smoke or CO detector surcharge: $3.00

Per LAHD, state law requires 30 days' written notice for increases under 10%.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement:
The act makes the following unlawful, each as a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act:
- for a rental property owner or its agent or subcontractor to pay for, subscribe to or contract for a coordinator's services
- for a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function
- for two or more persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination
- for a coordinator's agents to engage in parallel pricing coordination
- for any person to perform a coordinating function

A coordinating function means algorithmic or automated setting or recommending of rents, material lease terms or occupancy levels that either (1) uses nonpublic, competitively sensitive information of other owners, or (2) applies a common algorithm for two or more owners in a way that facilitates parallel pricing.

Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 to 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.

rules.title: Statewide prohibition on local rent control (G.L. c. 40P)
rules.requirement:
No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. The only exception is for a city or town that accepts chapter 40P, which may adopt rent control regulation subject to these limits:
- Owner compliance becomes entirely voluntary six months after initial adoption.
- The regulation may not cover occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal of properties from regulation.
- It may not apply to units of owners holding fewer than ten rental units, or to units with a fair market rent above $400.
- The municipality must compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent.

Rent control is defined to include any regulation that in any way requires below-market rents for residential properties.

rules.title: San Diego Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing (SDMC ch. 9, art. 8, div. 11)
rules.requirement:
It is unlawful for any person to sell, license or otherwise provide an algorithmic device to a landlord. It is also unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property.

An algorithmic device is software or a product that uses algorithms to calculate nonpublic competitor data of two or more landlords in order to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels for San Diego residential rental property.

Each month a landlord's use continues, and each property where a device is used, is a separate violation.

Tenants may sue a landlord for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. A prevailing landlord or tenant recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and lease clauses limiting fee recovery are unenforceable. Remedies are cumulative. The City may also enforce under SDMC ch. 1, art. 2, including civil and criminal remedies.

rules.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protections: just cause, relocation assistance, right to re-rent and buyout rules (SDMC ch. 9, art. 8, div. 7)
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not terminate a covered tenancy without just cause.

At-fault causes: nonpayment of rent, material lease breach, nuisance, waste, refusal to sign a substantially similar renewal (leases ending on or after June 24, 2023), criminal activity, criminal threats, unauthorized assignment or sublet, refusal of lawful entry, unlawful use, an employee's failure to vacate, and failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice. For a curable violation, the landlord must first give written notice and a chance to cure, and may then serve a three-day notice to quit.

No-fault causes, taken in good faith:
- Owner or relative move-in for at least 12 continuous months. For leases from June 24, 2023, the tenant must agree in writing or the lease must allow it. The occupant must move in within 90 days, otherwise the unit is re-offered at the same rent and terms.
- Withdrawal from the rental market.
- A government or court order or local ordinance requiring the unit to be vacated.
- Demolition or substantial remodel. Permits must be secured first, and the notice is certified under penalty of perjury with the specified contents.

No-fault notice: written, 30 or 60 days ahead per Civ. Code § 1946.1, in at least 12-point font. It must state the basis, the relocation right and the five-year right to an offer to re-rent.

Relocation assistance applies regardless of income or length of tenancy. It is 2 months of actual rent, or 3 months if the tenant is a senior (62+) or disabled. The landlord either pays it directly within 15 days of the notice or waives that amount of rent.

Right of first offer: if the unit is re-offered within 5 years of an eviction under § 98.0704(b)(1), (3) or (4), the displaced tenant gets the first offer if they asked in writing within 30 days. The tenant then has 30 days to accept.

Tenant notice: landlords must give every covered tenant the § 98.0705 rights notice and the Housing Commission's Tenant Protection Guide.

Commission notice: landlords must notify the Housing Commission of at-fault and no-fault terminations within 3 business days. This applies only from 30 days after the Commission announces a submission portal.

Buyouts: a written disclosure is required before any buyout offer. Buyout agreements must be in writing, contain the 14-point bold statements, be translated where required, and exceed the relocation amount, or they are void.

Retaliation is prohibited. Any noncompliance voids the termination notice.

rules.title: Hoboken Rent Control Ordinance: annual rent increase cap (lesser of 5% or CPI)
rules.requirement: At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not request or receive a rent increase greater than the lesser of 5% or the CPI percentage change. CPI is measured from three months before the lease commenced to three months before it expires or terminates. Periodic tenants, and tenants with leases under one year, cannot be charged more than one such increase in any 12-month period. Only one cost-of-living increase is allowed per housing space in any 12-month period, regardless of tenant turnover. Rents are controlled at the base rent received on October 1, 1985. Any increase made at a time other than lease expiration or termination, or above what the chapter allows, is void. Landlords must give at least 30 days' written notice explaining the reason for an increase. The notice must include a certification of substantial compliance with housing, building and fire codes, or it is invalid. Landlords must provide documented proof of previous rent paid to impose an increase. Landlords must also register annually by June 30 and give tenants a disclosure statement. Separately approved surcharges are allowed: tax, water/sewer, capital improvement (base rent may not rise more than 33 1/3% in 12 months) and hardship. On vacancy decontrol of a registered dwelling, the next tenant's initial rent is limited to a 25% increase over the prior rent, at most once in any three-year period. Violations are punishable under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5, including a fine of up to $2,000 per unit per violation.
rules.key_value: Rent increase capped at the lesser of 5% or the CPI percentage change (CPI measured from 3 months before lease commencement to 3 months before expiration); one increase per 12 months; 30 days' written notice with reasons; vacancy decontrol limited to a 25% increase on initial rent for the new tenant, once per 3 years; fines up to $2,000 per unit.

rules.title: Newark Rent Control Ordinance: annual CPI-based rent increase cap (max 4%)
rules.requirement: When a lease expires, or a periodic tenant's lease ends, a landlord may not request or receive an increase above the percentage change in the CPI-U for New York-northern New Jersey-Long Island. The change is measured from the CPI 15 months before the month of the proposed increase to the CPI 3 months before that month. The increase may never exceed 4%. Rent may not rise by more than this amount in any 12 consecutive months, regardless of tenant turnover, a change of ownership or vacancy. The landlord must give the tenant and the Rent Regulation Officer written notice at least 30 days ahead. The notice states the proposed increase and percentage, the prior year's rent, and the allowable increase amount and percentage. No annual increase is allowed if the dwelling is not in substantial compliance with codes or the landlord has not registered under § 19:2-9.8. Tax, major new improvement and utilities surcharges, and hardship increases, are separate Board processes. Board-granted increases within 12 months may not total more than 25%. Excess rent must be rebated, retroactive up to two years from the date of the petition. Violations bring fines of $100 to $2,000 and/or up to 90 days in jail, and the Board may impose penalties of up to $500.
rules.key_value: Annual increase capped at CPI-U change (15 months to 3 months before the increase), maximum 4%; one increase per 12 months; 30 days' written notice to tenant and Rent Regulation Officer; Board-granted increases capped at 25% per year
